Consult Summary:
- 48-year-old man with 3 days of frequent watery diarrhoea, central/sub‑umbilical crampy abdominal pain and one episode of vomiting; clinical impression in the consult was likely acute gastroenteritis (supportive DDx: viral > bacterial).

History:
- Presenting complaint:
  - Three days of diarrhoea with crampy central (sub‑umbilical) abdominal pain and one episode of vomiting this morning.
- Timeline:
  - Symptoms began ~3 days ago and have been persistent without clear improvement or worsening.
  - Vomited once this morning (patient believes it may have been previously eaten fruit).
- Exacerbating/relieving factors:
  - Frequent need to open bowels (every ~10 minutes); sensation of incomplete evacuation/need to go again after finishing.
  - Pain partially relieved after toileting; patient thinks some symptoms may represent trapped gas.
  - Patient is reducing oral intake because of nausea and frequent stools.
- Associated symptoms / review of systems:
  - Audible bowel sounds.
  - Mild abdominal tenderness on palpation.
  - Reports having been sweating a little over the past four days but no measured fever.
  - No chest pain or change in breathing beyond baseline asthma; ambulant and talking normally.
- Pertinent negatives:
  - No visible blood in stool or vomit (patient uncertain but believes vomiting contained strawberry only).
  - No syncope, severe systemic features, or breathing difficulty beyond baseline asthma.
  - No documented weight loss or chronic change in bowel habit discussed.

Past Medical History:
- Asthma — uses an inhaler (patient reports recently starting a new brand).
- Family history: father died ~10 years ago of bowel (colorectal) cancer.

Medications:
- Inhaler for asthma — dose/route/frequency not documented.
- No other regular medications documented.

Allergies:
- NKDA (patient reports "no known drug allergies").

Social History:
- Describes self as a foreigner.
- Not currently working at present due to symptoms; staying at home.
- Smoking, alcohol, and recreational drug use not documented.

Family History:
- Father deceased from bowel cancer approximately 10 years ago.

Physical Examination:
- Vitals: Not recorded.
- Examination findings:
  - Mild central abdominal tenderness on palpation (patient reports it hurts "a little bit" when pressed).
  - Audible bowel sounds reported by patient.
  - Otherwise patient ambulant, speaking normally; no acute respiratory distress beyond baseline asthma.
  - Full formal physical exam not recorded.

Investigations:
- No labs, imaging, or other investigations were ordered or reported during the consult.

Assessment & Plan:

Overall Impression:
- Working diagnosis: acute gastroenteritis, most likely viral in origin (consult impression). Bacterial foodborne illness is a secondary possibility; IBS and medication-related causes are less likely for an acute 3‑day presentation. Family history of colorectal cancer noted but unlikely to explain this acute illness.

DDx Integration (brief):
- Acute viral gastroenteritis — High likelihood.
  - Supporting: acute 3‑day watery diarrhoea, crampy central pain relieved somewhat by defecation, single vomit, no blood, patient not systemically very unwell.
  - Opposing: absence of documented fever (patient reported some sweating but no measured temperature) — not exclusionary.
- Bacterial gastroenteritis / food poisoning — Moderate likelihood.
  - Supporting: acute onset, high stool frequency, recent ingestion (fruit) and severe stool frequency.
  - Opposing: no fever, no bloody diarrhoea, no systemic toxicity documented.
- Irritable bowel syndrome (diarrhoea‑predominant) — Lower likelihood for this acute episode.
  - Supporting: crampy central pain relieved by defecation and sensation of incomplete evacuation.
  - Opposing: acute onset over days with vomiting—more suggestive of infectious cause.

Issue 1: Acute diarrhoea / presumed acute gastroenteritis
- Assessment:
  - Most consistent with acute gastroenteritis (likely viral); bacterial causes or food poisoning remain possible.
- Plan:
  - Conservative management advised in consult: maintain hydration (drink plenty of fluids / oral rehydration).
  - Monitor for fever and systemic deterioration.
  - Stay home/avoid work until improving.
  - Avoid antibiotics (doctor advised they usually do not help for this presentation).
  - Safety netting: seek in-person GP or urgent care if symptoms worsen (increasing abdominal pain, high fever, bloody stools, persistent vomiting / inability to keep fluids down, signs of dehydration), or if no improvement after a short interval (patient planned to wait 1–2 days then book GP).
  - No investigations or prescriptions were made during this consult.

Issue 2: Asthma / recent change of inhaler
- Assessment:
  - Asthma managed with inhaler; patient reports recently using a new inhaler and is concerned it may cause GI symptoms.
  - Clinician noted it is very unlikely an inhaler would cause this diarrhoeal picture.
- Plan:
  - Continue usual asthma care as previously advised by patient's asthma management plan (no change documented).
  - If patient has concerns about inhaler supply, technique, or side effects, arrange review with GP or pharmacist to clarify brand/contents and continue appropriate inhaler use.
  - Document inhaler details in future visits (dose/route/frequency not documented).

Issue 3: Family history of colorectal cancer — screening concern
- Assessment:
  - Significant family history (father died of bowel cancer) raises long-term screening consideration but is unlikely to account for this acute illness.
- Plan:
  - Reassure that current presentation is more consistent with infection; recommend discussion with GP for family history risk assessment and appropriate screening/timing if indicated (patient to book GP if symptoms persist or for routine care).
  - If recurrent or chronic change in bowel habit develops, arrange further evaluation in primary care.

General plan items:
- No tests or imaging arranged during this consult.
- Patient to monitor symptoms and seek in-person evaluation if worsening or if red‑flag features appear.
- Patient agreed to wait a day or two and book GP if not improving.

Quality checks:
- Missing but clinically expected elements: vital signs not recorded; medication details (inhaler dose/route/frequency) not documented; no formal abdominal exam findings beyond patient-reported mild tenderness; no stool/blood testing or lab data (none ordered).
- Conflicts between transcript and DDx: none significant; DDx supports the consult impression of acute gastroenteritis.
- Transcript quality: generally understandable; occasional brief hesitancy and minor clarification needed about dates/contents of vomit (patient uncertain whether vomit contained blood or strawberry); overall adequate for clinical synthesis.
